newsitem.title: CANADA: APEC countries to explore liberalizing air travel.
newsitem.headline: APEC countries to explore liberalizing air travel.

text.p: Transport ministers from Asia-Pacific countries agreed on Tuesday to work toward liberalizing air services in the region but set a cautious timetable for further action.

After a two-day meeting in Victoria, British Columbia, ministers from the 18-member Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum decided to consider late next year detailed options for liberalizing airline passenger and freight services.

"We all agreed we should work toward a more competitive aviation environment with fair and equitable access for all economies," Mah Bow Tan, Singapore's minister for communications, told reporters after the meeting. "...But we have to take into account that various economies are at various stages of development."

Canadian Transportation Minister David Collenette said an APEC working group will analyze ways to remove aviation barriers and submit its report to the transport ministers by mid-1998. Singapore's Mah said this report would help identify areas where progress can be made and also areas where "we will agree to disagree."

One of APEC's main drives is to free trade among member economies and more efficient transportation links are seen as an important way to underpin that effort, officials said. The ministers were meeting ahead of an APEC leaders' summit in Canada in November.

But APEC countries are divided over the merits of greater liberalization of air services. Countries in favor, such as the United States, point to the benefits of so-called "open-skies" agreements like the one between the United States and Canada that eliminate air travel barriers.
But some countries, including Japan, are reluctant to have foreign carriers gain full access to their markets.

"Liberalizing air services will not occur overnight, but we are forging ahead to better understand how trade liberalization will benefit all of APEC," U.S. Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater said after the APEC meeting.
"...The United States looks forward to entering open-skies agreements with all the economies in the Asia Pacific region that share the goals of open markets and unfettered opportunites."

Among the suggestions for further liberalization would be to expand bilateral air agreements between some countries to include cargo as well as passenger transport. Another idea is to let carriers set up their own ground support operations in foreign airports, something that is barred by some countries.
Some countries also want to allow airlines flying from one country to another to pick up passengers in a third country, a practice currently not permitted by some countries.

Slater and his Japanese counterpart, Makoto Koga, discussed a long-standing bilateral dispute over aviation on the sidelines of the APEC meeting. No concrete progress was reported from the talks but a U.S. official said both sides showed flexibility in their positions.

The United States wants an open skies agreement with Japan that eliminates government restrictions on aviation service, but Japan has opposed that idea. Negotiators from the two countries are scheduled to hold talks on the dispute next month.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States. Papua New Guinea did not send a minister to this week's meeting.
